extracted.intended_audience: students, poets, playwrights, critics and readers of classical poetics and rhetoric
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance drawn from Aristotle's Poetics, Longinus' On the Sublime, and Demetrius on Style about what makes good poetry, tragic drama, and elevated rhetoric — covering plot, character, diction, style, and effects on an audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mimesis (imitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry and drama are imitations (mimesis) of action and life rather than mere recounting of facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art should represent universal truth — the typical or probable — rather than particular historical fact; imitation must aim at what is meaningful about human action. Avoid mere chronicle; seek representations that reveal character and cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action (single, complete plot)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy should have a single unified action with a beginning, middle, and end forming a complete whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude extraneous subplots; every incident should contribute causally to the whole. The plot's completeness is judged by whether it produces catharsis and whether nothing essential is omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude/Scale (suitable size and seriousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot must be of suitable magnitude — large and serious enough to compel catharsis but compact enough to be grasped as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a scope that supports the gravity of emotion and moral significance without incoherence or triviality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability and Necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Events in the plot should follow from one another by probability or necessity rather than by chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer plausible causal chains; even surprising events must appear inevitable in retrospect. Avoid implausible coincidences that break the unity of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia (reversal) and Anagnorisis (recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Powerful plots often include a reversal of fortune (peripeteia) and a recognition (anagnorisis) that are causally connected and produce emotional effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design reversals and recognitions to arise naturally from the plot’s logic so they feel necessary and produce catharsis rather than artifices for shock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamartia (tragic flaw / error)
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist’s error, frailty, or mistaken action (hamartia) should plausibly lead to catastrophe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamartia must be humanizing and intelligible — not arbitrary wickedness. It should evoke both pity and fear in the audience by showing how good persons can err.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic Hero — goodness, propriety, and greatness
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic protagonist should be essentially good, fittingly noble or great, and consistent with human nature, so their fall arouses pity and fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid making the hero utterly virtuous (which removes credibility) or wholly villainous (which prevents pity). Their social status or greatness helps the magnitude of the fall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (ethos) — consistency and propriety
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should act in ways consistent with their established dispositions and social roles; speech and action must be appropriate to character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character revelation should arise from action; avoid inconsistent behaviour that serves plot convenience. Distinguish characters by manner of speaking and moral outlook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (dianoia) — themes and reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: The intellectual content — arguments, themes, and lines of thought — should be coherent, persuasive, and suited to the characters and plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thought appears through speeches and decisions; it must be credible and illuminate the moral and intellectual stakes of the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (lexis) — choice of words and phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Language must be apt, clear, and appropriate to subject and character; diction is a central part of artistic craft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metaphors and phrasing that are vivid and fitting; prefer clarity and force over ornate but empty ornament. Speech should differentiate character and elevate the subject where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphor and Figures of Speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Skillful metaphor and figures are essential to striking expression and to revealing truth poetically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective metaphors illuminate and fuse image with idea; avoid mixed or strained figures. Figures should be natural to the thought and strengthen precision and vividness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melos (song, meter, musical elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Musical elements (chorus, meter, lyric portions) contribute to the unity and emotional effect of tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate music and lyrical passages so they enhance mood and meaning rather than interrupt action. The chorus's lyrical function should support the plot and emotional contour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opsis (spectacle / visual effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacle — visible stage effects — can move the audience but is the least artistic element of tragedy according to classical critique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on spectacle sparingly; the plot, character, and language are primary. Spectacle should subordinate to and illuminate the action instead of masking weaknesses in plot or thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catharsis (emotional purification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy should produce catharsis — the purging or purification of pity and fear in the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange events to elicit these emotions genuinely through identification with the plot and protagonist; cheap shocks or melodrama that manufacture emotion without grounding reduce cathartic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot Structure: Beginning, Middle, End
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful work must have a clear beginning (that which does not presuppose other events), middle (that which follows and leads on), and end (that which follows from what precedes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure causal linkage so the beginning naturally leads to the middle and the middle to the end; avoid episodic fragments that lack teleology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of Style to Subject and Audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Style must fit the nature of the subject and the expectations of the audience — lofty subjects warrant elevated style; humble subjects call for plainness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose plain, middle, or grand style as suits the material; mismatches between subject and diction create dissonance or ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grandeur / Greatness of Thought (Longinus’ Sublimity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sublimity springs from greatness of thought — elevated, noble, and concentrated ideas that uplift the soul of the reader or audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for strong, expansive conceptions and images rather than petty or trivial preoccupations; cultivate imaginative scope and moral grandeur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passion and Emotional Force
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine passion, forceful feeling, and enthused delivery produce greatness of expression and move the audience profoundly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let feeling inform diction and structure; avoid manufactured or simulated emotion that lacks internal necessity. Passion should be controlled and directed by thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noble Diction and Elevated Expression
rubrics_metrics.description: A high style requires noble words and turns of phrase — dignified speech, apt metaphors, and cadenced periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate diction that is grand without being pompous; prefer clarity infused with loftiness. Avoid mean or low phrases in attempts to be sublime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figures, Tropes, and Rhetorical Ornament (Longinus/Demetrius)
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures of speech and rhetorical devices when used with judgment can amplify meaning and contribute to sublimity or beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ornament to illuminate thought, not to hide lack of substance. Well-chosen tropes (metaphor, antithesis, hyperbole where apt) increase vividness and emotional power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness and Spontaneity
rubrics_metrics.description: True sublimity and effective style appear natural and spontaneous rather than forced or mannered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursue effects that seem to flow inevitably from thought and feeling; avoid contrivance, artificial inversions, or overworked epithets that call attention to technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and Purity of Expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Even elevated language must preserve clarity; obscurity for its own sake undermines rhetoric and poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance loftiness with intelligibility; ambiguous or obscure phrasing that conceals meaning diminishes persuasive and emotional power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm, Cadence, and Musicality of Prose/Verse
rubrics_metrics.description: The measured flow of sentences or lines (rhythm, cadence) contributes to effect, dignity, and memorability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to sentence-period structure, balance, and sound; use varied rhythms to sustain interest and to underscore climactic moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness and Correctness (Demetrius)
rubrics_metrics.description: Correct grammar, proper use of words, and suitability of expressions are essential to good style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid solecisms, incorrect inflections, and misused terms; appropriateness includes register, grammatical correctness, and conventional propriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety, Freshness, and Avoidance of Commonplace
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective writing avoids stale or hackneyed turns of phrase and seeks fresh, apt expressions and images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for originality in metaphor and formulation; yet novelty must be intelligible and appropriate — novelty for its own sake can be alienating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and Force (concision without loss of richness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Powerful writing combines concentrated expression with sufficient richness; unnecessary prolixity weakens effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prune redundancy and prefer energetic, pointed statements; but do not sacrifice necessary detail or elevation required by the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrangement and Structure of Parts
rubrics_metrics.description: The order and disposition of parts (scenes, speeches, stanzas) must produce the intended intellectual and emotional rise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange episodes so that tension accumulates and resolves; place emphatic material at structurally significant points; transitions should be smooth and motivated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical and Moral Seriousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry and tragedy should engage moral and human questions with seriousness appropriate to their form — frivolity undermines tragic dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat human conduct with gravity; moral confusion or trivialization of serious themes reduces the work’s ethical and cathartic power.
